q: Which compound is the strongest Brønsted acid?
h: All four acidic hydrogens sit on atoms in the same molecule type (CH<sub>3</sub>–X–H). Compare the atoms X: across a row, then down a group.
w: Going down a group, atom size outweighs electronegativity: the S–H bond is longer and weaker, and the negative charge of CH3S− is spread over a larger, more polarizable atom. CH3SH (pKa ≈ 10) is therefore more acidic than CH3OH (≈ 15.5). Across the second row, acidity follows electronegativity: O–H > N–H (CH3NH2, ≈ 40) > C–H (ethane, ≈ 50).
x: Methanol (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 15.5) is the most acidic of the second-row compounds, but sulfur is below oxygen and size wins down a group, so methanethiol is about 10<sup>5</sup> times more acidic.
Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sup>−</sup> is much less stable than CH<sub>3</sub>O<sup>−</sup>; methylamine (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 40) is a very weak acid.
Ethane (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 50) puts the negative charge on carbon, the least electronegative atom here, so it is the weakest acid of the four.

q: Rank compounds I–IV in order of increasing acidity (weakest acid first).
h: Ask what stabilizes each conjugate base: which atom carries the charge, and can it be delocalized by resonance?
w: Ethane (II, pKa ≈ 50) leaves the charge on carbon. Ethanol (IV, ≈ 16) puts it on oxygen with no resonance. Phenol (III, ≈ 10) puts it on oxygen with delocalization into the ring (onto carbons). Acetic acid (I, ≈ 4.8) delocalizes the charge over two oxygens, the best case. Order: II < IV < III < I.
x: This places ethanol above phenol. Ethoxide has no resonance, while phenoxide spreads its charge into the ring, so phenol (pK<sub>a</sub> 10) is about a million times more acidic than ethanol (16).
Ethane cannot be more acidic than ethanol: a carbanion on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 50) is far less stable than an alkoxide (≈ 16).
Phenoxide delocalizes charge onto ring carbons, but acetate delocalizes it onto a second oxygen, which is better; acetic acid (4.8) is more acidic than phenol (10).

q: Which labeled hydrogen (on atom a, b, c or d) is the most acidic?
h: Recall the approximate pK<sub>a</sub> of each type: terminal alkyne C–H, alcohol O–H, ketone α-C–H, phenol O–H.
w: Approximate pKa values: a terminal alkyne ≈ 25; b primary alcohol ≈ 16; c ketone α-hydrogen ≈ 20; d phenol ≈ 10. The phenoxide ion has the charge on oxygen and delocalized into the aromatic ring, so the phenol O–H on d is the most acidic, about 106 times more acidic than the alcohol.
x: Atom b is an ordinary alcohol (pKa ≈ 16); its alkoxide has no resonance stabilization, unlike phenoxide.
The ketone α-hydrogen (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 20) gives a resonance-stabilized enolate, but the charge starts on carbon; it is about 10<sup>10</sup> times less acidic than the phenol.
The sp C–H of a terminal alkyne (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25) is acidic for a hydrocarbon, but far weaker than any O–H in this molecule.

q: Acetic acid (pK<sub>a</sub> 4.8) is mixed with one equivalent of sodium ethoxide; ethanol has pK<sub>a</sub> 16. Which best describes the equilibrium shown?
c: It lies far to the right; K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>11</sup>
It lies far to the left; K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>−11</sup>
It lies to the right; K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 3
It lies far to the right; K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>21</sup>
h: Find the acid on each side. The equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid, and K<sub>eq</sub> = 10<sup>(pK<sub>a</sub> of product acid − pK<sub>a</sub> of reactant acid)</sup>.
w: The reactant acid is acetic acid (4.8); the product acid is ethanol (16). Equilibrium favors the weaker acid (and weaker base), so it lies to the right. Keq = 10(16 − 4.8) = 1011.2, so far to the right, Keq ≈ 1011. The Na+ counterion is a spectator and is not written.
x: This subtracts in the wrong order. The stronger acid (acetic acid) is on the left, so the reaction proceeds forward and K<sub>eq</sub> > 1.
This divides the pK<sub>a</sub> values (16/4.8 ≈ 3). pK<sub>a</sub> values are logarithms, so K<sub>eq</sub> comes from their difference as a power of ten.
This adds the two pK<sub>a</sub> values. K<sub>eq</sub> depends on the difference, 16 − 4.8 = 11.2.

q: Which base can deprotonate 1-hexyne (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25) essentially completely?
h: A base works well only if its conjugate acid is a weaker acid (higher pK<sub>a</sub>) than the compound being deprotonated.
w: For complete deprotonation, the conjugate acid of the base must have a higher pKa than the alkyne. Only NaNH2 qualifies: NH3 (≈ 38) is a much weaker acid than the alkyne (25), so Keq ≈ 1013. This is why acetylide ions are made with NaNH2.
x: Water (15.7) is a stronger acid than the alkyne (25), so hydroxide gives K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>−9</sup>; almost no acetylide forms.
Methanol (≈ 15.5) is a stronger acid than the alkyne, so methoxide gives K<sub>eq</sub> ≈ 10<sup>−10</sup>.
Bicarbonate is a very weak base (its conjugate acid has pK<sub>a</sub> 6.4); it can deprotonate carboxylic acids but not alkynes.

q: Solid NaNH<sub>2</sub> is added to water. Which statement best describes the result?
c: NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> is converted essentially completely to NH<sub>3</sub>, and OH<sup>−</sup> becomes the strongest base present.
NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> stays the strongest base present, because Na<sup>+</sup> stabilizes it as an ion pair.
Very little reaction occurs, because NH<sub>3</sub> is a stronger acid than water.
NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> removes a proton from H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> only, so the solution stays neutral.
h: Compare the pK<sub>a</sub> of water (15.7) with that of NH<sub>3</sub> (≈ 38). What is the strongest base that can survive in water?
w: Water (pKa 15.7) is a far stronger acid than NH3 (≈ 38), so NH2− + H2O → NH3 + OH− has Keq ≈ 1022. This is the leveling effect: any base stronger than OH− is converted to OH− in water, so OH− becomes the strongest base present. Strong bases such as NaNH2 must be used in solvents that are weaker acids than their conjugate acids (for example liquid NH3).
x: Na<sup>+</sup> is a spectator counterion; it does not change which side of a proton transfer is favored. Amide ion is destroyed by water.
This reverses the acidities: water (15.7) is about 10<sup>22</sup> times more acidic than NH<sub>3</sub> (≈ 38).
The H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> concentration in neutral water is tiny (10<sup>−7</sup> M); NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> reacts with water itself and the solution becomes strongly basic.

q: Boron trifluoride dissolves in diethyl ether to form the adduct shown. Which statement is correct?
c: Diethyl ether is the Lewis base, and boron in the adduct has a formal charge of −1.
Diethyl ether is the Lewis base, and boron in the adduct has a formal charge of +1.
BF<sub>3</sub> is the Lewis base, and oxygen in the adduct has a formal charge of −1.
Diethyl ether is the Lewis acid, and boron in the adduct has a formal charge of −1.
h: Which species has an empty orbital, and which has a lone pair? Then find formal charges: B (four bonds, no lone pairs) and O (three bonds, one lone pair).
w: BF3 has an empty 2p orbital on boron (only six valence electrons), so it is the electron-pair acceptor (Lewis acid). The ether oxygen donates a lone pair, so ether is the Lewis base. In the adduct, boron has four bonds and no lone pairs: FC = 3 − 4 = −1; oxygen has three bonds and one lone pair: FC = 6 − 2 − 3 = +1.
x: The donor/acceptor roles are right, but boron with four bonds and no lone pairs has formal charge 3 − 0 − 4 = −1, not +1; the +1 belongs to oxygen.
BF<sub>3</sub> accepts the electron pair, so it is the Lewis acid; the fluorine lone pairs are not used in this bond. Oxygen in the adduct is +1.
The ether gives up a lone pair to boron, which makes it the Lewis base, not the Lewis acid.

q: Rank phenols I–IV in order of increasing acidity (weakest acid first).
h: In the phenoxide ion, the negative charge reaches the ortho and para carbons by resonance, but not the meta carbons. Which substituents can accept that charge, and from which position?
w: Phenoxide charge is delocalized to the ortho and para carbons. A para-NO2 (II, pKa ≈ 7.2) can take the charge directly onto its oxygens by resonance and withdraw inductively. A meta-NO2 (IV, ≈ 8.4) withdraws only inductively, because the charge never reaches the meta carbon. Phenol itself (I) is ≈ 10. A para-OCH3 (III, ≈ 10.2) donates electron density by resonance, destabilizing the anion slightly. Order: III < I < IV < II.
x: This makes meta-nitrophenol more acidic than para. Only the para nitro group can delocalize the phenoxide charge onto its own oxygens by resonance, which outweighs the slightly closer inductive effect of a meta group.
Methoxy oxygen is electronegative, but at the para position its resonance donation dominates; 4-methoxyphenol is slightly less acidic than phenol, not more.
This is the order of decreasing acidity (strongest first), the reverse of what was asked.

q: Which ranking lists acids I–IV from most acidic to least acidic?
h: All four are carboxylic acids, so the carboxylate resonance is the same. Look at where (or whether) the electron-withdrawing Cl sits relative to the COOH.
w: An electronegative chlorine stabilizes the carboxylate by inductive withdrawal, and induction falls off quickly with the number of bonds. Chlorine on C2 (III, pKa ≈ 2.9) has the largest effect, on C3 (I, ≈ 4.1) less, on C4 (IV, ≈ 4.5) little, and butanoic acid (II, ≈ 4.8) has none: III > I > IV > II.
x: This reverses the distance effect. Induction weakens with each bond, so a Cl far from the carboxylate (IV) helps least, not most.
This swaps I and IV. Chlorine on C3 is one bond closer to the carboxylate than chlorine on C4, so I is more acidic than IV.
Butanoic acid has no electron-withdrawing group and is the weakest acid of the set, not the strongest.

q: Which carbanion is the most stable (the weakest base)?
h: Each lone pair sits in a hybrid orbital on carbon. More s character holds electrons closer to the nucleus.
w: The acetylide ion (HC≡C−) holds its lone pair in an sp orbital (50% s character), close to the nucleus, which stabilizes it. That is why ethyne (pKa 25) is far more acidic than ethene (≈ 44) or ethane (≈ 50). Its conjugate acid is the strongest, so the anion is the weakest base.
x: The vinyl anion's lone pair is in an sp<sup>2</sup> orbital (33% s); it is more stable than an alkyl anion but much less stable than acetylide (pK<sub>a</sub> of ethene ≈ 44).
The ethyl anion has its lone pair in an sp<sup>3</sup> orbital (25% s), far from the nucleus; ethane's pK<sub>a</sub> is about 50.
Alkyl groups are weakly electron-donating, so a tertiary carbanion is even less stable than a primary one; carbanion stability runs opposite to carbocation stability.

q: Which labeled hydrogen is the most acidic?
h: Deprotonate each carbon in your head. Over how many electronegative atoms can the resulting charge spread?
w: Removing H from carbon b, between two C=O groups, gives an anion delocalized onto both carbonyl oxygens (pKa ≈ 9, like 2,4-pentanedione). Carbon c is α to only one carbonyl (pKa ≈ 20), the alkyne C–H on a is ≈ 25 (no resonance, only sp character), and the CH3 on d is β to the carbonyl, so its anion has no resonance (≈ 50). Answer: carbon b.
x: Carbon c is α to only one carbonyl, so its enolate spreads the charge onto one oxygen (pKa ≈ 20). Carbon b is α to two.
The terminal alkyne C–H (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25) is stabilized only by sp hybridization, which is weaker than delocalizing the charge onto two oxygens.
Carbon d is β to the carbonyl, not α; the anion cannot be delocalized onto oxygen, so this is an ordinary alkane C–H.

q: Ethanol reacts with sodium hydride to give sodium ethoxide and hydrogen gas. Why does this reaction go essentially to completion?
c: H<sup>−</sup> is a very strong base (pK<sub>a</sub> of H<sub>2</sub> ≈ 36), and H<sub>2</sub> escapes as a gas.
Na<sup>+</sup> binds ethoxide tightly, which drives an otherwise unfavorable proton transfer.
H<sup>−</sup> attacks carbon as a nucleophile and displaces ethoxide from ethanol.
Ethanol is a stronger acid than water, so any base deprotonates it completely.
h: Compare the pK<sub>a</sub> of ethanol with that of the conjugate acid of hydride. Then ask what happens to that conjugate acid once it forms.
w: The conjugate acid of H− is H2 (pKa ≈ 36), far weaker than ethanol (≈ 16), so Keq ≈ 1020. In addition, H2 bubbles out, so the reverse reaction cannot occur. NaH therefore makes alkoxides cleanly; Na+ is just the counterion.
x: Na<sup>+</sup> is a spectator counterion. The large pK<sub>a</sub> difference, not the cation, makes the reaction favorable.
Hydride from NaH acts as a base, not a nucleophile, and ethanol has no leaving group at carbon (OH<sup>−</sup> is a poor leaving group anyway). The products are ethoxide and H<sub>2</sub>.
Ethanol (≈ 16) is in fact slightly weaker than water (15.7), and a weak base such as NaHCO3 does not deprotonate it at all.

q: A tert-butyl carbocation reacts with water to give the oxonium ion shown. In this step, which species acts as the Lewis acid?
c: The carbocation, which accepts an electron pair
Water, which donates an electron pair to carbon
Water, which donates a proton to the carbocation
The oxonium ion, which accepts a proton from water
h: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair. Which reactant has an empty orbital?
w: The carbocation has an empty p orbital and accepts a lone pair from the water oxygen, so the carbocation is the Lewis acid (electrophile) and water is the Lewis base (nucleophile). No proton moves in this step.
x: Donating an electron pair makes water the Lewis base, not the Lewis acid.
No proton is transferred in this step; a bond forms from an oxygen lone pair to the carbocation carbon.
The oxonium ion is the product of this step; it loses a proton later, acting as a Brønsted acid, not as a Lewis acid that accepts one.

q: Phenol (pK<sub>a</sub> 10.0) is mixed with sodium acetate (pK<sub>a</sub> of acetic acid 4.8). What is the approximate K<sub>eq</sub> for the reaction shown?
h: K<sub>eq</sub> = 10<sup>(pK<sub>a</sub> of the product acid − pK<sub>a</sub> of the reactant acid)</sup>.
w: The reactant acid is phenol (10.0) and the product acid is acetic acid (4.8). Keq = 10(4.8 − 10.0) = 10−5.2 ≈ 10−5. The stronger acid (acetic acid) is on the right, so the equilibrium lies to the left: acetate is too weak a base to deprotonate phenol.
x: This has the sign reversed. The weaker acid (phenol) is on the reactant side, so the equilibrium favors reactants and K<sub>eq</sub> < 1.
This adds the pK<sub>a</sub> values (10 + 4.8 ≈ 15). K<sub>eq</sub> uses their difference.
This divides the pK<sub>a</sub> values (4.8/10). pK<sub>a</sub> values are logarithms; their difference becomes an exponent of 10.

q: Which anion is the strongest base?
h: The strongest base has the weakest conjugate acid (highest pK<sub>a</sub>). Recall the pK<sub>a</sub> of ethanol, acetic acid, ammonia and ethyne.
w: Conjugate-acid pKa values: ethanol ≈ 16, acetic acid ≈ 4.8, NH3 ≈ 38, ethyne ≈ 25. The highest belongs to NH3, so the amide ion, NH2−, is the strongest base. This is why NaNH2 deprotonates terminal alkynes.
x: Ethoxide (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 16) is a strong base but about 10<sup>22</sup> times weaker than amide ion.
Acetate is resonance-stabilized; its conjugate acid has pK<sub>a</sub> 4.8, making it the weakest base here.
Acetylide (conjugate acid pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25) is a strong base, but amide is stronger; that is exactly why NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup> can make acetylide ions.
